tasks.title: Reading a Sort-Merge Join Plan

description.context: A teammate joins NordGrid's 12M-row meters Silver layer to the 3M-row customer_master dimension and shows you the .explain() output. They ask you to confirm the join strategy, count the shuffles, and explain why Spark made this choice rather than broadcasting customer_master.
description.task: How many shuffles does this plan trigger, and what is the strongest signal in the plan that confirms the join strategy?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Description: Both sides are large enough that broadcast is not a candidate. Customer_master is roughly 280MB compressed in Parquet, well above the default 10MB autoBroadcastJoinThreshold.

Left Size: 12M rows (meters Silver, ~3.4GB compressed)

Right Size: 3M rows (customer_master, ~280MB compressed)

Broadcast Threshold: 10MB (default)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 12M-row meters table joined to 3M-row customer_master on customer_id

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
result = meters.join(customer_master, on='customer_id', how='inner')
result.explain()

fields.label: How many shuffles does this plan trigger, and what is the strongest signal in the plan that confirms the join strategy?
options: One shuffle — Spark shuffles only the larger side because the join key already exists on the smaller side; the SortMergeJoin operator in the plan confirms the strategy because broadcast was rejected for size

Two shuffles — both Exchange hashpartitioning operators repartition by customer_id; SortMergeJoin is the strongest signal that Catalyst chose sort-merge over broadcast because both sides exceed the threshold
Three shuffles — each Sort operator triggers a global sort which involves a shuffle, plus the join itself; the SortMergeJoin signal indicates Catalyst applied a worst-case strategy here

Zero shuffles — AdaptiveSparkPlan with isFinalPlan=false means AQE has not yet executed the plan, so the Exchange operators are placeholders that AQE will skip if it converts the join to broadcast at runtime
fields.correctAnswer: Two shuffles — both Exchange hashpartitioning operators repartition by customer_id; SortMergeJoin is the strongest signal that Catalyst chose sort-merge over broadcast because both sides exceed the threshold
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Counts only one shuffle.Sort-merge joins always shuffle both sides — that is what 'merge' requires (co-located partitions).

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lesson 4 (Reading SortMergeJoin plans), PSI3 lesson 2 (Broadcast threshold and strategy choice).

tasks.title: Aggregate Before Join, or Join Before Aggregate

description.context: Two engineers solve the same problem: produce per-region average daily_kw with substation metadata. Snippet A joins meters (12M rows) to substations (120 rows) first, then aggregates. Snippet B aggregates meters first, then joins. Both produce identical output. The question is which is faster and why.
description.task: Which snippet is faster on a 12M-row meters dataset, and why?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Description: meters: 12M rows, key columns include substation_id, region, daily_kw. substations: 120 rows (~50KB), well below autoBroadcastJoinThreshold.

Meters Size: 12M rows

Substations Size: 120 rows (broadcast-eligible)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 12M-row meters joined to 120-row substations

fields.label: Which snippet is faster on a 12M-row meters dataset, and why?
options: Snippet A is faster because the broadcast of substations happens once before any aggregation work; the post-join groupBy operates on enriched data without shuffling the substation columns separately

Snippet A is faster because Spark cannot broadcast substations after a groupBy stage; the broadcast-eligibility check happens before the first wide transformation in the plan and a groupBy disqualifies later joins from broadcast

Both are equivalent in Catalyst because the optimizer reorders aggregate-vs-join freely when the join key is the same as the groupBy key; the engineer's choice of order is decorative when statistics are accurate

Snippet B is faster because the groupBy reduces meters from 12M rows to ~120 rows BEFORE the join — the join then operates on a tiny aggregated DataFrame; aggregation is a row-reducer and reducing before joining is almost always cheaper
fields.correctAnswer: Snippet B is faster because the groupBy reduces meters from 12M rows to ~120 rows BEFORE the join — the join then operates on a tiny aggregated DataFrame; aggregation is a row-reducer and reducing before joining is almost always cheaper
fields.rationale: Aggregate-first wins by a substantial margin.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Misjudges the dominant cost.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 5 (Aggregate-Join Reordering and Row-Reduction Strategies).

tasks.title: BroadcastExchange — What Does the Plan Show?

description.context: A teammate joins meters (12M rows) to substations (120 rows) with a simple .join() call — no explicit broadcast hint. They show you the .explain() output and ask what the plan reveals about Spark's strategy choice.
description.task: What is the strongest signal in this plan, and what mechanism placed BroadcastExchange above only one side of the join?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Description: Meters is the large side; substations is the small side at ~50KB compressed in Parquet, well below the 10MB autoBroadcastJoinThreshold.

Left Size: 12M rows

Right Size: 120 rows (~50KB compressed)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 12M-row meters joined to 120-row substations on substation_id

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
result = meters.join(substations, on='substation_id', how='inner')
result.explain()

fields.label: What is the strongest signal in this plan, and what mechanism placed BroadcastExchange above only one side of the join?
options: BroadcastHashJoin with BuildRight indicates the right side (substations) was selected as the build side; BroadcastExchange above only that side prepares the broadcast — Catalyst chose this strategy because substations is below the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold

The single Exchange operator on the meters side indicates a shuffle; BroadcastExchange is a separate physical operator unrelated to broadcast — it represents Spark's mode of broadcasting a small reference table to executors after the shuffle has already happened

BroadcastHashJoin with BuildRight indicates Catalyst broadcasted both sides; the absence of an Exchange on the meters side confirms that Catalyst chose to skip the meters shuffle by replicating both DataFrames to every executor for an in-memory hash join

The plan shows a fallback strategy because broadcast was attempted but failed at runtime; BroadcastExchange is the operator Spark uses when it had to materialize the broadcast on disk after the in-memory broadcast exceeded the executor heap
fields.correctAnswer: BroadcastHashJoin with BuildRight indicates the right side (substations) was selected as the build side; BroadcastExchange above only that side prepares the broadcast — Catalyst chose this strategy because substations is below the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold
fields.rationale: Two cues in the operator name carry most of the meaning: the strategy chosen by Catalyst, and which DataFrame is the build side.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Inverts what BroadcastExchange means.BroadcastExchange IS the broadcast preparation, not a separate post-shuffle step.

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lesson 5 (Reading Broadcast Join plans), PSI3 lesson 3 (BroadcastExchange semantics and BuildRight/BuildLeft).

tasks.title: The Broadcast Hint That OOMed the Driver

description.context: An engineer added .hint('broadcast') to a customer_master join eight months ago. The pipeline ran fine in dev (5,000 customer rows in the test fixture) and ran fine in production for months. Last week the pipeline started failing with a driver OOM. Customer_master has grown organically as new customers were enrolled — it is now 2.4GB in production. The engineer asks you to diagnose.
description.task: What is the bug, and what is the correct alternative?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Description: Customer_master grew from 5K rows in dev to 3M rows in production over 8 months; total compressed size 2.4GB.

Dev Size: 5,000 rows (~250KB)

Prod Size: 3,000,000 rows (~2.4GB)

Driver Heap: spark.driver.memory=4g (default 1g + 3g override from cluster config)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 12M-row meters joined to 3M-row customer_master (at production scale)

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

# 8 months ago, when customer_master was 5K rows in dev:
result = meters.join(broadcast(customer_master), on='customer_id', how='inner')

# Today, customer_master is 3M rows; this raises:
# org.apache.spark.SparkException: Job aborted due to stage failure: 
# Task 0 in stage 12.0 failed: ExecutorLostFailure ... Container killed by YARN 
# for exceeding memory limits. Used 4.2 GB of 4 GB physical memory.

fields.label: What is the bug, and what is the correct alternative?
options: The hint forces customer_master to be collected to the driver in full before being shipped to executors; the 4GB driver heap cannot hold the 2.4GB build-side hashed relation, so the OOM occurs during BroadcastExchange. Removing the hint lets Catalyst pick sort-merge based on the threshold

The bug is the executor's hash table running out of memory while building the broadcast structure; the engineer should increase spark.executor.memory to accommodate the 2.4GB customer_master and keep the broadcast hint, since broadcast is still architecturally correct for a dimension table

The hint disables AQE's runtime conversion to sort-merge once the actual shuffle sizes are known; the engineer should remove the hint and rely on AQE to choose the strategy at runtime, with spark.sql.adaptive.enabled and the local-shuffle-reader settings doing the work

The bug is that broadcast hints implicitly assume the build side fits in the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold even when explicitly hinted; the engineer should keep the hint but explicitly raise spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 4GB so Catalyst no longer rejects the broadcast at planning time
fields.correctAnswer: The hint forces customer_master to be collected to the driver in full before being shipped to executors; the 4GB driver heap cannot hold the 2.4GB build-side hashed relation, so the OOM occurs during BroadcastExchange. Removing the hint lets Catalyst pick sort-merge based on the threshold
fields.rationale: Broadcast hints OVERRIDE the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold check.Catalyst sees the hint and commits to broadcasting the hinted side regardless of size.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Confuses driver-side OOM with executor-side OOM.Broadcast preparation happens on the driver; the failure is on the driver heap.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 4 (Broadcast Hints and Driver-Side Build), PSI3 lesson 6 (Statistics-Driven Strategy and the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold).

tasks.title: Why Both Sides Shuffle

description.context: A teammate joins meters (12M rows) to events (4M rows) on (region, date). Both tables are large enough that broadcast is not a candidate. The plan shows a SortMergeJoin with two Exchange operators and two Sort operators. The teammate asks why both sides shuffle when they could imagine a strategy where only one side moves.
description.task: Why does Spark shuffle both sides when one might intuitively be enough — and what role do the Sort operators play?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Description: Both DataFrames are large; neither is below the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold. The join is on a composite key (region, date).

Left Size: 12M rows (meters)

Right Size: 4M rows (events)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 12M-row meters joined to 4M-row events on (region, date)

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
result = meters.join(events, on=['region', 'date'], how='inner')
result.explain()

fields.label: Why does Spark shuffle both sides when one might intuitively be enough — and what role do the Sort operators play?
options: The Sort operators (false flag) are the actual shuffles between executors, while the Exchange operators are redundant placeholders that AQE will remove at runtime; only one shuffle on the larger meters side actually occurs

The engine hashpartitions left and right by (region, date) into the same 200 buckets so matching keys end up co-located on a single executor; the false-flag step performs within-partition reordering — required because sort-merge needs rows in key order to advance in a single pass

Spark shuffles both sides because the join condition contains two columns; a single-column join would shuffle only the side whose partitioning does not already match, but composite keys always require both sides to repartition because no partition layout can satisfy both columns simultaneously

The two Exchange operators materialize the join condition on disk before the merge; if the join were broadcast, the plan would still show two Exchanges but one would be marked as broadcast — SortMergeJoin confirms broadcast was rejected
fields.correctAnswer: The engine hashpartitions left and right by (region, date) into the same 200 buckets so matching keys end up co-located on a single executor; the false-flag step performs within-partition reordering — required because sort-merge needs rows in key order to advance in a single pass
fields.rationale: Co-location is the structural requirement that drives both shuffles.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Inverts the meaning of Sort's false flag.

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lesson 4 (SortMergeJoin operator anatomy), PSI3 lesson 2 (Co-location and shuffle requirements).

tasks.title: Missing Statistics Force Sort-Merge

description.context: Two .explain() outputs of the same query are shown side by side. The query joins meters (12M rows) to a 'tariffs_extended' reference table that is 80MB in production — well below the 10MB autoBroadcastJoinThreshold... wait, 80MB is ABOVE the default 10MB threshold. Let us assume the cluster has spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold=128MB. The first plan was captured before ANALYZE TABLE COMPUTE STATISTICS was run on tariffs_extended; the second was captured after.
description.task: What changed between Plan A and Plan B, and what is the platform-engineering lesson?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Description: tariffs_extended is 80MB compressed, structurally broadcast-eligible at 128MB threshold. The difference between the two plans is whether Catalyst can SEE that size.

Tariffs Size: 80MB compressed

Broadcast Threshold: 128MB (cluster-overridden from default 10MB)

Before State: no statistics computed

After State: ANALYZE TABLE tariffs_extended COMPUTE STATISTICS executed

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 12M-row meters joined to 80MB tariffs_extended; cluster threshold raised to 128MB

fields.label: What changed between Plan A and Plan B, and what is the platform-engineering lesson?
options: Plan A was sort-merge because tariffs_extended exceeded the 10MB default threshold; Plan B switched to broadcast because spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold was raised to 128MB between the two captures, making the table newly eligible

Plan B's broadcast was triggered by a hidden broadcast() hint that ANALYZE TABLE silently injected as part of the statistics computation; Spark's statistics command updates query plans as a side effect, which is why Plan A reverted to sort-merge

AQE intervened in Plan B and switched the strategy at runtime once the actual shuffle sizes were observed; the same query would produce Plan A both times if AQE were disabled in the cluster, regardless of whether statistics were computed for the table

The strategy switched because Catalyst could not estimate tariffs_extended's size without statistics; ANALYZE TABLE produced them, Catalyst saw 80MB against the 128MB threshold, and chose broadcast. Lesson: statistics on join columns affect plans even when data has not changed
fields.correctAnswer: The strategy switched because Catalyst could not estimate tariffs_extended's size without statistics; ANALYZE TABLE produced them, Catalyst saw 80MB against the 128MB threshold, and chose broadcast. Lesson: statistics on join columns affect plans even when data has not changed
fields.rationale: Catalyst's broadcast eligibility check requires it to KNOW the size of each side.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Invents a threshold change.The scenario explicitly states the threshold is 128MB throughout.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 6 (Statistics-Driven Strategy Choice), PSI3 lesson 7 (Maintaining Statistics on Join Columns).

tasks.title: Per-Task Shuffle-Read Distribution

description.context: A teammate's join pipeline runs significantly slower than expected. They show you the Spark UI's Stage page for the join shuffle stage. The 200-task histogram is heavily skewed: 198 tasks read between 30MB and 60MB each, but two tasks read 4GB and 6GB respectively. They ask you to interpret what this distribution tells you and which join key is likely driving it, given NordGrid's known customer_type distribution.
description.task: What does this distribution indicate, and which key value is most likely driving the skew?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Description: 200-task shuffle stage. The Spark UI shuffle-read histogram is dominated by two outlier tasks. NordGrid's customer_type distribution is RESIDENTIAL 60%, COMMERCIAL 25%, INDUSTRIAL 12%, PROSUMER 3%.

Task Count: 200

Median Shuffle Read: ~50MB

P99 Shuffle Read: ~6GB

Outlier Count: 2

Outlier Sizes: 4GB, 6GB

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Spark UI per-task shuffle-read distribution from a join on customer_type

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
# Spark UI Stage page — Shuffle Read Size per Task
# Tasks  Min      25%      50%      75%      Max
# 200    28MB     45MB     52MB     58MB     6GB
# 
# Tasks 0-197: 30-60MB each
# Task 198: 4GB
# Task 199: 6GB
#
# Pipeline: meters.join(customer_type_dim, on='customer_type', how='left')

fields.label: What does this distribution indicate, and which key value is most likely driving the skew?
options: The distribution indicates random task placement variance; modest skew is expected on any large cluster, and the 4GB/6GB tasks reflect normal hash partition imbalance from the 200 hash buckets used by Catalyst's default shuffle partition count

The distribution suggests a corrupted shuffle file; the two outlier tasks are reading additional data because of replication after a node failure during the prior shuffle write — the engineer should re-run the stage with retry enabled

Classic skew on the join key — RESIDENTIAL at 60% concentrates into one hash bucket and COMMERCIAL at 25% into another; the two outlier tasks correspond to those two key values, while the other 198 tasks handle smaller customer_type subsets and shuffled-empty buckets

The distribution reflects join-side imbalance — meters has more rows than customer_type_dim, so the meters-side tasks read disproportionately large shuffle volumes while customer_type_dim-side tasks read small volumes; the 4GB/6GB tasks are meters-side tasks
fields.correctAnswer: Classic skew on the join key — RESIDENTIAL at 60% concentrates into one hash bucket and COMMERCIAL at 25% into another; the two outlier tasks correspond to those two key values, while the other 198 tasks handle smaller customer_type subsets and shuffled-empty buckets
fields.rationale: Skew is the canonical interpretation of this shape.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats 100× imbalance as 'normal variance'.Random partitioning produces near-uniform distribution; this magnitude is structural skew.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 8 (Detecting Skew from Per-Task Shuffle Read Distributions), PSI3 lesson 9 (Customer-type skew at NordGrid).

tasks.title: The Salt That AQE Silently Invalidated

description.context: An engineer added hand-rolled salting to a customer_type join nine months ago to handle the known 60/25/12/3 skew. The pipeline worked correctly when AQE was disabled in the cluster. After the platform team enabled AQE by default last month, the same pipeline started producing rows with NULL on the customer_type-aware columns — not consistently, but enough to fail downstream validation. The engineer asks you to identify the bug.
description.task: What is the bug that surfaced after AQE was enabled, and what is the correct fix?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Description: The engineer salts customer_type by appending a random 0-9 suffix on the meters side, then joins to a customer_type_dim that has been replicated 10× (one row per (customer_type, salt_value) pair).

Salt Factor: 10

Aqe State: enabled in cluster default since 2026-04-15

Failure Mode: intermittent NULLs in customer_type_dim columns post-join

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Hand-rolled salting code interacting with AQE-enabled cluster

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, expr, lit, concat

# Salt the meters side: append random 0-9 suffix to customer_type
salted_meters = meters.withColumn(
    'customer_type_salted',
    concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'), (expr('rand() * 10').cast('int')))
)

# Replicate the dim side: 10 rows per customer_type, one per salt value
salted_dim = (customer_type_dim
    .crossJoin(spark.range(10).withColumnRenamed('id', 'salt'))
    .withColumn(
        'customer_type_salted',
        concat(col('customer_type'), lit('_'), col('salt').cast('int'))
    ))

# Join on the salted key
result = salted_meters.join(
    salted_dim,
    on='customer_type_salted',
    how='left'
)
# Production: intermittent NULLs in salted_dim columns post-join

fields.label: What is the bug that surfaced after AQE was enabled, and what is the correct fix?
options: AQE's coalesce-shuffle-partitions step reduced the partition count below 10, mapping multiple salt values to the same partition; the salt's pre-condition (each salt value lives on its own partition) was invalidated. The fix is to disable AQE for this stage, or remove the salt and rely on AQE's automatic skew handling instead

AQE's skew-handling intervention split the skewed partition further; the split fragments do not all contain the corresponding dim-side rows, producing missed matches on the affected partitions. The fix is to disable spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled while keeping the rest of AQE enabled

The expr('rand() * 10') call is non-deterministic across stages; AQE's runtime re-execution of the salting step produces different salt values than the dim side received, so some salted_meters rows have salts that the dim side never produced. The fix is to use a deterministic hash of an existing column instead of rand()

The crossJoin call disables AQE on the dim side via Spark's broadcast-fallback policy; the dim side is partitioned differently from the meters side after the crossJoin, breaking salt alignment. The fix is to call .repartition('customer_type_salted', 10) on the dim side before the join
fields.correctAnswer: The expr('rand() * 10') call is non-deterministic across stages; AQE's runtime re-execution of the salting step produces different salt values than the dim side received, so some salted_meters rows have salts that the dim side never produced. The fix is to use a deterministic hash of an existing column instead of rand()
fields.rationale: Non-determinism in the salt expression is the root cause.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Confuses partition count with salt cardinality.Salting embeds the salt in the data; partition count is independent.

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lesson 10 (Salting and AQE Interaction), PSI3 lesson 11 (Deterministic vs Non-Deterministic Expressions in Spark Plans).

tasks.title: Plan-Reading Pipeline With Three Joins

description.context: You are reviewing a daily-billing-prep pipeline that joins meters to three reference tables. The code runs and produces correct output. The teammate has captured the .explain() output and asks you to walk through the plan with them. Read both the snippet (lines numbered) and the plan excerpt, then answer the questions.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 12M-row meters joined to substations (120 rows), customer_master (3M rows), tariffs (12 rows)

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, sum, broadcast

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("daily_billing_prep").getOrCreate()

# Bronze inputs
meters = spark.read.parquet("silver/meters/")            # 12M rows
subs = spark.read.parquet("reference/substations/")      # 120 rows
customers = spark.read.parquet("reference/customer_master/")  # 3M rows
tariffs = spark.read.parquet("reference/tariffs/")        # 12 rows

# Step 1: enrich with substation metadata
step1 = meters.join(subs, on="substation_id", how="inner")

# Step 2: enrich with customer master
step2 = step1.join(broadcast(customers), on="customer_id", how="left")

# Step 3: enrich with tariff price
step3 = step2.join(tariffs, on="customer_type", how="left")

# Step 4: aggregate per region
result = (step3
    .withColumn("revenue", col("daily_kw") * col("eur_per_kw"))
    .groupBy("region", "date")
    .agg(sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue_eur")))

result.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("date").parquet("gold/daily_revenue/")

tasks.pssReference: PSI1 lessons 4-5 (Reading multi-join plans), PSI3 lessons 3-4 (Broadcast hints and AQE coalesce).

tasks.title: The Pipeline With Five Mid-Level Join Bugs

description.context: Final exercise of the track. A mid-level engineer's daily-billing pipeline runs without errors and ships output that downstream consumers accept. Three weeks after a cluster reconfiguration, Finance reports that monthly revenue is off by 4.2% and one nightly run took 3.5 hours instead of the usual 35 minutes. Investigation traces the divergence to five mid-level join mistakes in the same pipeline. Read the code (line numbers shown) and identify each.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 12M-row meters, 3M-row customer_master, 120-row substations, 12-row tariffs, 600K-row historical_meters self-join

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, sum, broadcast

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("daily_billing").getOrCreate()

# Bronze inputs
meters = spark.read.parquet("silver/meters/2026-04-*")           # 12M rows
subs = spark.read.parquet("reference/substations/")               # 120 rows
customers = spark.read.parquet("reference/customer_master/")     # 3M rows, 280MB
tariffs = spark.read.parquet("reference/tariffs/")                # 12 rows
historical = spark.read.parquet("silver/meters_historical/")    # 600K rows, prior month

# Step 1: substation enrichment with explicit broadcast
step1 = meters.join(broadcast(meters), on="substation_id", how="inner")

# Step 2: customer enrichment - sort-merge expected
step2 = step1.join(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")

# Step 3: tariff lookup via self-join on customer_type
tariff_lookup = (meters
    .filter(col("date") == "2026-04-01")
    .select("customer_type", "daily_kw")
    .alias("a")
    .join(meters.alias("b"), on="customer_type", how="inner"))

# Step 4: revenue calc with tariffs (joined here, late)
step3 = step2.join(tariffs, on="customer_type", how="left")

# Step 5: month-over-month comparison via second customers join
step4 = step3.join(historical, on="meter_id", how="left")
step5 = step4.join(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")

# Step 6: revenue and aggregate
result = (step5
    .withColumn("revenue", col("daily_kw") * col("eur_per_kw"))
    .groupBy("region", "customer_type", "date")
    .agg(sum("revenue").alias("daily_revenue_eur")))

result.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("date").parquet("gold/daily_revenue/")

tasks.pssReference: PSI3 lessons 4, 6, 7 (broadcast hint mechanics, statistics-driven planning, join order optimization).
